blocks.html:
READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Deep sea discovery

Recent research has provided new insights into how fish communicate.

Nico Michiels is an ecologist from the University of Tübingen in Germany who spends part of each year in Egypt, where he dives in the Red Sea, observing fish life and gathering data on its coral reefs. In September 2007 he decided to find out how far red light could penetrate the ocean depths. Seawater absorbs different colours at different depths, and as an experienced diver, Michiels was aware that red light is extinguished not far below the surface whereas blue-green light penetrates deeper. To find out the depth at which red disappeared in this particular ocean, however, he attached a special plastic filter to his dive mask, which was designed to block out all colours except red. Then he began to descend. In theory, once he reached about 15 metres, he should have been plunged into darkness. Instead, something totally unexpected happened. Sure enough, 20 metres down it was as dark as night. ‘All the fish disappeared. With no light from the surface, they were effectively black and had become invisible,' he says. ‘But it didn't stay black for long. Then I saw a group of goby fish with bright red eyes lit up against the background. After that, red spots began to show up all over the reef.'

Even with the red filter removed, Michiels could pick them out without much trouble once his eyes grew accustomed to the gloom. It seems strange that no diver or researcher had spotted all this red before, but as Michiels points out, no one saw it because no one expected to see it. On that one dive, Michiels discovered three fish species with prominent red markings, and has found many others since.

But how can fish appear red where there's no red light? Ordinary red pigments* look red because they reflect red light while absorbing all other wavelengths. At 20 metres down, there had to be some other explanation for the red Michiels was seeing. He suspected fluorescence. Fluorescent pigments behave differently from ordinary ones: they receive incoming light of one wavelength, for example blue, and emit light of a longer wavelength, in this case red. On the reef in the Red Sea during daytime, the most likely explanation was that the predominantly blue and green wavelengths at depth triggered the emission of fluorescent red in the fish.

*pigments: a pigment is a substance that gives something a particular colour.

With only a week left in Egypt, and lacking the equipment to confirm that the fish were fluorescent, Michiels photographed as many of them as he could. Then, once back in Germany, he bought an assortment of tropical fish and installed them in his lab. Here he confirmed that the fish did indeed fluoresce. In most of the fish he looked at, the fluorescence could be traced to specialised pigment cells that lie in the skin beneath the scales. These cells contain 'guanine crystals', which scatter light to give fish their silvery sheen. However, Michiels says they are still not sure exactly what is fluorescing. ‘It's not the crystals themselves. It's probably a fluorescent protein built into the crystals, and we have a suspicion that it might be made by bacteria.'

Intrigued, Michiels began a systematic search for red fluorescence in reef fish. He and his colleagues, Nils Anthes and Dennis Sprenger, have identified some 50 species with red fluorescence. The most common markings tend to be on the body towards the head and to a lesser extent around the eyes, and then the fins. To Michiels, the distribution of these markings is one of the strongest indications that red fluorescence has a very particular function: communication with other members of the species. According to several recent studies, a whole range of animals employ fluorescence as a natural highlighter to boost the visibility of body parts they use to signal, for example to ward off enemies. In reef fish, the red tends to be confined to parts of the body used to signal, suggesting these markings serve a similar function. But instead of highlighting an existing colour, the fluorescence gives the fish a colour that otherwise wouldn't exist. For example, fish commonly use eye rings to signal that they are present and their direction of gaze, and Michiels suspects that red-eyed gobies use signals to indicate their location and keep their group together.

Red light, whatever its source, doesn't travel far through water, which suggests signals are intended to be private, seen only by nearby fish of the right species. There are several lines of evidence to support this, says Michiels. And closely related species do not have completely identical markings, which suggests they might be important in species recognition.

Michiels suspects red fluorescence has another important role for some reef fish: helping them blend in. During his first dive with the red filter, he noticed corals glow a dark but faint red too. Against this irregular red background, a fish that glows red all over would be hard to distinguish. More compelling for Michiels is the case of the scorpionfish, which lies perfectly still until food swims past, which it then sucks in.

Yet if red plays any part in a fish's life, then it must be able to see it. Fish that live in a world dominated by blue-green light are assumed to have eyes tuned to those wavelengths, and most marine fish that have been studied are thought incapable of seeing red. One exception is the seahorse, whose eyes are sensitive to red. As for the other fish, it remains to be seen.

questionGroups.bodyHtml:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?

In boxes 1–6 on your answer sheet, write:

  • TRUE if the statement agrees with the information
  • FALSE if the statement contradicts the information
  • NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this

1 During his 2007 dive, Michiels expected to encounter total darkness at about 15 metres.

2 Michiels could see the red markings on fish without the aid of the red filter.

3 Other divers had assumed they would see fish with red markings.

4 All the fish with red markings that Michiels found during his diving expeditions came from the Red Sea.

5 Michiels first thought of the possibility that fish could fluoresce while he was in Germany.

6 Michiels remains uncertain as to what creates fluorescence in fish.

Complete the notes below.

Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.

Michiels's findings

Michiels has observed:

  • 50 types of fish with red fluorescence in total
  • markings mainly near the 7

Some of Michiels's beliefs are that:

  • red fluorescence is used specifically for 8 purposes
  • fish, like some animals, use fluorescence to keep 9 away
  • gobies depend on red fluorescence to show their 10
  • there are variations in the markings of fish among those 11 which are very similar

Other benefits of red fluorescence:

  • fish cannot easily be seen near backgrounds of 12 which give off a red light
  • helps some fish catch their prey

The ability to see red amongst fish:

  • the only fish proven to have this ability is the 13

passageNotes.label: 第一段
passageNotes.text: 尼科·米歇尔斯是德国图宾根大学的一位生态学家，他每年都会花一部分时间在埃及，在红海潜水，观察鱼类生活并收集其珊瑚礁的数据。2007年9月，他决定找出红光能穿透海洋多深。海水在不同深度吸收不同颜色的光，作为一名经验丰富的潜水员，米歇尔斯知道红光在离水面不远处就会消失，而蓝绿光则能穿透得更深。然而，为了找出红光在这个特定海洋中消失的深度，他在潜水面罩上附加了一个特殊的塑料滤光片，该滤光片旨在阻挡除红色外的所有颜色。然后他开始下潜。理论上，一旦他到达约15米，他应该会陷入黑暗。然而，完全出乎意料的事情发生了。果然，在20米深处，天色漆黑如夜。“所有的鱼都消失了。没有来自水面的光，它们实际上是黑色的，变得看不见了，”他说。“但它并没有一直保持黑暗。然后我看到一群虾虎鱼，它们的亮红色眼睛在背景中亮了起来。之后，红色的斑点开始在整个礁石上显现出来。”

passageNotes.label: 第二段
passageNotes.text: 即使取下红色滤光片，一旦他的眼睛习惯了昏暗的环境，米歇尔斯也能毫不费力地把它们辨认出来。似乎很奇怪，以前没有潜水员或研究人员发现过所有这些红色，但正如米歇尔斯指出的那样，没有人看到它是因为没有人期望看到它。在那次潜水中，米歇尔斯发现了三种带有显著红色标记的鱼类，此后又发现了许多其他种类。

passageNotes.label: 第三段
passageNotes.text:
但是在没有红光的地方，鱼怎么能呈现红色呢？普通的红色素\*之所以看起来是红色的，是因为它们反射红光而吸收所有其他波长的光。在20米深处，米歇尔斯看到的红色一定有其他解释。他怀疑是荧光。荧光色素的行为与普通色素不同：它们接收一种波长的入射光，例如蓝色，然后发出更长波长的光，在这种情况下是红色。在白天红海的珊瑚礁上，最可能的解释是，深处主要的蓝色和绿色波长的光触发了鱼体内荧光红的发射。
\*色素：色素是一种赋予某物特定颜色的物质。

passageNotes.label: 第四段
passageNotes.text: 在埃及只剩下一周时间，并且缺乏确认鱼类是否发荧光的设备，米歇尔斯尽可能多地拍摄了它们的照片。然后，一回到德国，他买了一批热带鱼并把它们安置在他的实验室里。在这里，他确认了这些鱼确实会发荧光。在他观察的大多数鱼中，荧光可以追溯到位于鳞片下方皮肤中的特殊色素细胞。这些细胞含有“鸟嘌呤晶体”，它们散射光线，赋予鱼类银色的光泽。然而，米歇尔斯说，他们仍然不确定究竟是什么在发荧光。“不是晶体本身。很可能是一种内置于晶体中的荧光蛋白，我们怀疑它可能是由细菌制造的。”

passageNotes.label: 第五段
passageNotes.text: 受到好奇心的驱使，米歇尔斯开始系统地寻找珊瑚礁鱼类中的红色荧光。他和他的同事，尼尔斯·安特斯和丹尼斯·斯普伦格，已经识别出大约50个带有红色荧光的物种。最常见的标记倾向于出现在朝向头部的身体上，其次是在眼睛周围，然后是鳍部。对米歇尔斯来说，这些标记的分布是红色荧光具有非常特殊功能的最有力迹象之一：与同物种的其他成员进行交流。根据几项最近的研究，各种各样的动物都利用荧光作为一种天然的荧光笔来增强它们用于发信号的身体部位的可见度，例如为了驱赶敌人。在珊瑚礁鱼类中，红色往往局限于用于发信号的身体部位，这表明这些标记具有类似的功能。但荧光不是增强现有颜色，而是赋予鱼类一种否则不存在的颜色。例如，鱼类通常使用眼环来表明它们的存在和注视方向，米歇尔斯怀疑红眼虾虎鱼使用信号来指示它们的位置并保持群体在一起。

passageNotes.label: 第六段
passageNotes.text: 红光，无论其来源如何，在水中传播不远，这表明信号是私密的，只能被附近同种的鱼看到。有几条证据支持这一点，米歇尔斯说。而且亲缘关系很近的物种并没有完全相同的标记，这表明它们可能在物种识别中很重要。

passageNotes.label: 第七段
passageNotes.text: 米歇尔斯怀疑红色荧光对某些珊瑚礁鱼类还有另一个重要作用：帮助它们融入环境。在他第一次带红色滤镜潜水时，他注意到珊瑚也发出暗淡但微弱的红色光。在这种不规则的红色背景下，一只全身发红光的鱼将很难被分辨出来。对米歇尔斯来说，更有说服力的是蝎子鱼的例子，它会一动不动地躺着，直到食物游过，然后把它吸进去。

passageNotes.label: 第八段
passageNotes.text: 然而，如果红色在鱼的生活中扮演任何角色，那么它必须能看到它。生活在一个以蓝绿光为主的世界里的鱼，被认为眼睛已适应那些波长，而已被研究的大多数海洋鱼类被认为无法看到红色。一个例外是海马，它的眼睛对红色敏感。至于其他鱼，还有待观察。

items.text:
(1) 题目 1：During his 2007 dive, Michiels expected to encounter total darkness at about 15 metres. （在2007年的那次潜水中，米歇尔斯预计在大约15米处会遇到一片漆黑。）
答案：TRUE
解析：A段说“In theory, once he reached about 15 metres, he should have been plunged into darkness”，与题干的“expected”意思一致。

(2) 题目 2：Michiels could see the red markings on fish without the aid of the red filter. （不用红色滤镜，米歇尔斯也能看到鱼身上的红色标记。）
答案：TRUE
解析：B段明确说“Even with the red filter removed, Michiels could pick them out...”。

(3) 题目 3：Other divers had assumed they would see fish with red markings. （其他潜水员原本就以为能看到带红色标记的鱼。）
答案：FALSE
解析：B段说“no one saw it because no one expected to see it”，与题干相反。

(4) 题目 4：All the fish with red markings that Michiels found during his diving expeditions came from the Red Sea. （米歇尔斯在潜水考察中发现的所有带红色标记的鱼都来自红海。）
答案：NOT GIVEN
解析：B段只说他在红海的一次潜水中发现了三种，之后又发现了许多其他种类，但未说明这些“其他种类”的发现地点。

(5) 题目 5：Michiels first thought of the possibility that fish could fluoresce while he was in Germany. （米歇尔斯是在德国时第一次想到鱼可能会发荧光。）
答案：FALSE
解析：C段描述他在20米深处观察时就“suspected fluorescence”，这是在红海潜水时产生的想法。

(6) 题目 6：Michiels remains uncertain as to what creates fluorescence in fish. （对于是什么产生了鱼的荧光，米歇尔斯仍不确定。）
答案：TRUE
解析：D段末尾引用他的话说“they are still not sure exactly what is fluorescing”，明确表达了不确定性。

items.text:
(1) 题目 7：markings mainly near the 7 \___\___ （标记主要位于7 \___\___附近。）
答案：head
解析：E段说标记倾向于“on the body towards the head”。

(2) 题目 8：red fluorescence is used specifically for 8 \___\___ purposes （红色荧光被专门用于8 \___\___目的。）
答案：communication
解析：E段说红色荧光的功能是“communication with other members of the species”。

(3) 题目 9：fish, like some animals, use fluorescence to keep 9 \___\___ away （鱼类，像一些动物一样，利用荧光来驱离9 \___\___。）
答案：enemies
解析：E段举例说动物利用荧光“to ward off enemies”。

(4) 题目 10：gobies depend on red fluorescence to show their 10 \___\___ （虾虎鱼依靠红色荧光来显示它们的10 \___\___。）
答案：location
解析：E段说虾虎鱼用信号“to indicate their location”。

(5) 题目 11：there are variations in the markings of fish among those 11 \___\___ which are very similar （在那些非常相似的11 \___\___中，鱼的标记存在差异。）
答案：species
解析：F段说“closely related species do not have completely identical markings”。

(6) 题目 12：fish cannot easily be seen near backgrounds of 12 \___\___ which give off a red light （在会发出红光的12 \___\___背景附近，鱼不易被看见。）
答案：corals
解析：G段提到“corals glow a dark but faint red”，在这种背景下鱼很难被分辨。

(7) 题目 13：the only fish proven to have this ability is the 13 \___\___ （目前唯一被证实有这种能力的鱼是13 \___\___。）
答案：seahorse
解析：H段明确指出一个例外是“the seahorse, whose eyes are sensitive to red”。
